abstract.p: Applying magnetic resonance methods to measure the metabolic response in exercise poses a technical challenge because the construction of the ergometer must use non-magnetic components and assess work in the confined space of a magnet bore. The present report details the fabrication of a non-magnetic ergometer for use in a standard Siemens 3 Tesla (T) spectrometer. Using the ergometer, researchers can measure the 31P magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS) signals during leg muscle exercise and exercise recovery. In particular, the phosphocreatine (PCr) kinetics during exercise recovery reflects the mitochondrial oxidative capacity, and the inorganic phosphate (Pi) signal tracks the cellular pH. The ergometer allows for the use of a personalized, and variable load that normalizes the work for all study participants regardless of their leg strength. The ergometer then enables a standardized MRS comparison of leg muscle bioenergetics.

list-item.p: A non-magnetic ergometer enables researchers to use magnetic resonance imaging/spectroscopy (MRI/MRS) methods to measure the metabolic changes of exercising human muscle in vivo as a function of work.
The drawing and specifications provide a blueprint for researchers to fabricate the ergometer.

31P NMR measurements monitor the muscle bioenergetics during an exercise/exercise recovery protocol and demonstrate the utility of the ergometer in following muscle bioenergetics during and after exercise.
The ergometer allows the researcher to set the work level relative to the maximum voluntary contraction (MVC).

Using the ergometer and MRI/MRS methods allows researchers to determine the contrasting mitochondrial functions in normal and compromised muscle in patients suffering from different diseases, such as chronic kidney disease, and to assess the efficacy of therapeutic intervention.

sec.title: Background
sec.p: Many experiments utilize the phosphocreatine recovery (PCr) kinetics after exercise to determine the muscle mitochondria performance. These magnetic resonance (MR) studies often employ a free kick protocol in which the subject kicks freely and rapidly with no weight attached to the leg and with no set cadence [1]. During the exercise (∼ 1 min) the PCr decreases to 20–30% of the control level. During recovery, the PCr returns to its control level with characteristic kinetics. The free kick approach, however, overlooks the range of muscle power output in normal and in subjects with different medical conditions, such as chronic kidney disease, and limits the comparative analysis with different physiological parameters. Consequently, evaluating any therapeutic intervention can become clouded. Developing a non-magnetic ergometer that defines the exercise work output relative to the maximal voluntary contraction (MVC) for subjects with medical conditions enables the proper correlation of the PCr recovery kinetics with work output. The non-magnetic ergometer enables then an assessment of therapeutic intervention to improve muscle bioenergetics.

sec.title: Data Description
sec.p: The data comprise of 7 figures showing the design specification of the ergometer, the positioning of the subject's leg in the ergometer, the placement of the ergometer with the subject in an MRS/MRI scanner, the detection of 31P MRS signals during the exercise-recovery protocol, the nonlinear fit to determine the exponential rate constant in the PCr recovery kinetics, and the pH profile. The table summarizes the observed 31P MRS data and the analysis of the PCr recovery kinetics in one subject with repeated measurements (n=3) to test for precision and reproducibility.

Fig. 1 shows the ergometer built from non-magnetic material (wood, plastic, aluminum). The ergometer fits into a commonly available 3T Siemens scanner where MRI/MRS methods can then follow the metabolism in exercising muscle.Fig. 1
Front view photograph of the ergometer.Fig 1

Fig. 2 shows the position of the subject's leg in the ergometer. The slider, a sliding component, rests on the subject's ankle. As the subject's leg kicks, the foot pushes against the slider and raises it toward a stop plate. The slider's travel distance from rest to the stop plate defines a critical parameter in calculating work. A weight placed on the foot sets the workload.Fig. 2
Illustration of the leg position in the ergometer with the slider and weight resting on the ankle.Fig 2

Fig. 3 shows the ergometer positioned in a 3-T scanner. A surface coil resting on top of the leg detects the MRS signal during and after exercise. Slots in the ergometer allow straps to anchor the unit to the scanner bed.Fig. 3
Photograph of a subject on the MR scanner bed: Straps hold the ergometer to the bed. The subject's foot goes underneath the slider. An ankle weight rests on the ankle. A cushion under the knee provides support for the leg as it kicks. A 31P/1H surface coil rests on the quadriceps and monitors the changes in 31P signal from the muscle during exercise and exercise recovery.Fig 3

Fig. 4 shows the time resolved 31P MRS spectra from human quadriceps before, during, and after exercise. Each spectrum corresponds to an averaged signal acquired every 6 s as the subject kicks at 1 Hz against a load approximating 10% of maximal voluntary contraction (MVC).Fig. 4
A representative set of 31P spectra collected from the experiments during rest, exercise, and postexercise recovery. These experiments tested the ergometer's performance and showed reproducibly in securing the same PCr recovery kinetics during postexercise.Fig 4

Select spectra before, during, and after exercise show the signals of PCr at −2.54 ppm; inorganic phosphate (Pi) at 2.30 ppm; and γ-ATP, ⍺-ATP, and β-ATP at −4.81 ppm, −10.00 ppm, −18.50 ppm, respectively, Fig. 5.Fig. 5
A select group of spectra corresponding to A) rest, B) exercise, and C) postexercise recovery. The signal at -2.54 ppm arises from phosphocreatine (PCr), at 2.30 ppm from inorganic phosphate (Pi), and at -4.81 ppm, -10.00 ppm, -18.50 ppm from γ-ATP, ⍺-ATP, and β-ATP, respectively.Fig 5

Fig. 6 shows the modeling of the PCr recovery kinetics after exercise using the exponential equation:PCr(t)=PCr(0)+ΔPCr(1−e−kt)where t = time; k = rate constant; PCr(0) = [PCr] at the beginning of exercise recovery; ΔPCr = PCr (rest)-PCr (0) [2,3]. Studies have established that the rate constant of PCr recovery kinetics reflects the muscle mitochondrial bioenergetics in broad range of subjects, including those with chronic kidney disease [1].Fig. 6
Nonlinear fit of the PCr recovery kinetics after exercise using the exponential equation:PCr(t)=PCr(0)+ΔPCr(1−e−kt)where t = time; k = rate constant; PCr(0) = [PCr] at the beginning of exercise recovery; ΔPCr = PCr(rest)-PCr(0). Solid black circles represent all collected data (n=3). Time zero on the x-axis corresponds to the beginning of exercise recovery. Upper and lower bounds indicate 95% confidence intervals.Fig 6

Solid black circles represent all collected data (n=3). Time zero on the x-axis corresponds to the beginning of exercise recovery. PCr drops an average of 27.4±3.8% from its resting level at the start of recovery. The exponential rate constant for PCr recovery is 1.53±0.10 min−1. Upper and lower bounds demarcate the 95% confidence interval.

Fig. 7 displays the pH profile as reflected in the chemical shift of the Pi peak, as calculated from the equation:pH=6.75+logδo−δAδB−δowhere δo = observed chemical shift of the Pi signal; δA = ppm of [H2PO41−] at 3.290 ppm, δB = ppm of [HPO42−] at 5.805 ppm. The PCr signal at −2.54 ppm serves as the chemical shift reference.Fig. 7
PH profile derives from the chemical shift of the Pi peak and from the equation:pH=6.75+logδo−δAδB−δo,where δo = observed chemical shift of the Pi signal; δA = ppm of [H2PO41−] at 3.290 ppm, and δB = ppm of [HPO42−] at 5.805 ppm.Fig 7

After the control period, the exercise begins and continues for 42 s. A recovery phase follows for the next 360 s. The control pH of 7.00±0.01 shifts insignificantly to 7.01±0.02 at the end of exercise and the beginning of recovery and to 6.97±0.02 at the end of exercise.

sec.title: Subjects
sec.p: The study was reviewed and approved by the Human Subjects Welfare Committee of the University of California, Davis. One subject was recruited from the university as an untrained volunteer to test the reproducibility (n=3) of the 31P MRS measurement before, during, and after exercise in a 3T MRS/MRI scanner.

sec.title: Ergometer design
sec.p: The design required 1.91 cm (¾ in) marine plywood to construct an 18.42 cm × 25.04 cm × 34.24 cm (7.25 in × 10.25 in × 13.48 in) box with an open top, which has a 12.7 cm × 14.94 cm (5.00 in × 5.88 in) piece bridging the 2 sides. Glue and dowels joined all the pieces. The open frame of the box contained 2 plastic grooves that allowed a slider to move from its resting position to a final position determined by the stop plate. Positioning the stop plate required moving 2 aluminum rods into holes pre-drilled with a spacing resolution of 1.91 cm (0.75 in) in the ergometer's sides. Initially, the slider would rest on the subject's ankle, which may have an ankle weight resting on it to define the workload. Kicking the slider to the stop plate defined the travel distance. The slider can travel 17.53 cm (6.9 in) from its resting position. The subject kicked at 1 Hz for 42 s.

sec.title: Maximal voluntary contraction
sec.p: The MVC determination used a Biodex Isokinetic Dynamometer System 4 (Biodex SystemX, Biodex Medical Systems, Shirley, NY) and Biodex Advantage software (Biodex Medical System, System 4 Pro) to measure the performance of the right quadriceps [4,5]. Participants sat upright with their right knee joint aligned with the dynamometer's axis of rotation. The Biodex dynamometer leg attachment length was adjusted so the ankle pad was secured above the right malleolus. Participants were secured to the seat according to a standard Biodex procedure using shin, right thigh, pelvic, and upper-crossing torso stabilization straps. Three MVC trials of 3 s maximal-effort contractions separated by 10 s of passive rest at a knee-joint angle of 90° were performed. Participants were told to contract their right leg as hard as possible, while trying to push their leg away. Maximal peak torque in Newton-meter (N·m) was measured for each trial. The best of the three maximal peak torques was recorded as leg maximal isometric muscle strength, which was converted into unit of kilogram.

sec.title: Subject positioning in the MR scanner
sec.p: The subject was positioned supine and feet-first on the spectrometer bed. A cushion rest underneath the knee to create about a 40° bend referenced to the neutral position aligning the greater trochanter with the lateral malleolus. Positioning the subject slightly toward the left edge of the bed allowed the right quadriceps to better approach the magnet isocenter. An image marker was placed on their right quadricep muscle approximately half-way between the knee and hip.

Given the participant's Biodex-determined MVC, a weight was placed on the ankle to target 5–10% MVC. The ankle weight was strapped over a thin cushion pad around the participant's right ankle and was further secured with Velcro tape. A half-cylinder foam was placed under the right knee joint to create the required bend. Small sandbags were placed to better position the foot. The ergometer was then secured to the scanner bed with two web straps.

A PulseTeq 31P/1H surface coil (PulseTeq, Chobham, Woking, United Kingdom) was secured on top of the leg adjacent the quadriceps (about halfway between the knee and thigh joint). The subject was asked to kick a few times to check that the surface coil, ankle weight, and ergometer did not move. Ankle weights could be as low as 5% MVC. The weight, % MVC, and the kicking distance values were noted to ensure consistency in total work in subsequent experiments.

sec.title: MRS/MRI protocol
sec.p: The project conducted the MRI/MRS experiments in 2 phases and used both the 3T (123.25 MHz) Siemens Trio or Prisma scanner (Munich, Germany). In the 1st phase, the body coil imaged the quadriceps using a multi-slice transverse and sagittal T1-weighted images, and obtained Dixon transverse images, which separated the water and fat signals using a 3D gradient-echo sequence (3DGRE) protocol. A 3-plane localizer image first defined the subject's position in the scanner. An automatic shim routine improved the magnetic field homogeneity. A T1 and a Dixon imaging protocol followed.

The T1 imaging protocol contained the following acquisition parameters: TR (repetition time) = 600 ms; slice thickness=5 mm; in phase echo time=19 ms, number of scans=2, number of slices = 50, matrix size= 256×256 points; spatial resolution=1.1×1.1 mm3. The Dixon image protocol used the following parameters: recycle time (TR) = 22 ms; slice thickness=5 mm; in phase echo time=2.4, 3.6, 4.8, 6.0, 7.2, 8.4; and 9.6 ms, out of phase echo time = 1.5, 3.0, 4.5, 6.0, 7.5, 9.0, 10.4 ms; number of scans (NS)=2, number of slices = 36, field of view (FOV)=220×220 cm; matrix size= 128×128 points; spatial resolution=1.7×1.7 mm3; readout gradient=monopolar.

In the 2nd phase, shimming with the 31P/1H surface coil (PulseTeq) further improved the magnetic field homogeneity. The coil then detected the 31P NMR signals from the quadriceps before, during, and after exercise. 31P NMR spectra collected at 48.89 MHz used the following parameters: NS = 1; points = 2,000; spectral width = 2 KHz. The first 4 spectra were collected with a TR = 10 s. The second set of spectra was collected with a TR = 1.0 s.
Signal averaging 6 transients produced a spectrum corresponding to a specific time point. Each transient requires 1 s of signal acquisition.

sec.title: Exercise
sec.p: The subject was informed of the exercise protocol and listened for the start signal to begin exercising. During the control period, the subject did not move. Upon receiving the start signal, the subject began to use the ergometer to kick at 1 Hz in the ergometer for 42 s. The exercise targeted a PCr drop between 20–30%. When the subject received a stop signal, the subject stopped kicking. For the next 6 min after exercise cessation, the subject did not move in the scanner, but the MRS experiment continued to follow the 31P NMR signal during exercise recovery.

sec.title: NMR Data analysis
sec.p: JMRUI version 6.0 (MRUI Consortium, European Union) processed the spectra with an exponential line broadening of 10 Hz. The current data set showed a reproducible PCr drop of 27%. Typically, the PCr should drop between 20–30% during exercise. Keeping a moderate exercise intensity ensures that the muscle pH does not become acidotic.
